compareCandidate.label: Conservation of mass vs. balancing
compareCandidate.description: Conservation of mass is the LAW — matter is never created or destroyed. Balancing an equation is the SKILL — choosing coefficients so the written equation matches the law. The law is the truth; balancing is how we write it correctly.

parts: Matter is never created or destroyed
processes: Guaranteeing equal mass on both sides
plainLanguageExplanation: The law of conservation of mass is one of the great rules of nature: in any chemical reaction, matter is never created and never destroyed. It only changes form. Imagine you burn a piece of wood. The wood turns to ash and smoke, and it seems like matter disappeared — but it did not. The carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms in the wood and the air simply rearranged into new substances: ash, smoke, and gases. If you could weigh every product of the fire — the ash, the smoke, the gases — together they would weigh exactly as much as the wood plus the oxygen that fed the fire. Every atom present at the start is present at the end. This is why chemical equations must be balanced: the same number of each kind of atom must appear on both sides. The atoms are the conservation. A chemical reaction is not a magic trick that makes matter vanish — it is a reshuffling of the same atoms into new combinations. Mass in equals mass out, always.

whyItMatters: Conservation of mass is the bedrock law that makes all chemistry trustworthy. It lets chemists balance equations, predict exactly how much product a reaction will yield, and understand that matter transforms — but never vanishes. It explains everything from burning fires to breathing to rusting metal.
didYouKnow: When you burn a log, the total weight of the fire's products is GREATER than the log's weight — because oxygen from the air joined the reaction. The log was never the whole story.
compareReason: Conservation of mass is the law and balancing is the skill that obeys it — comparing them shows why equations must match reality.
